scenario_stem:
Glenmore Dairy Co is a private limited company in Country X making fresh milk and yoghurt for 9 supermarket chains. General manager Ravi Menon leads 46 employees across pasteurising, packing and quality control, processing 18,500 litres of milk a day. Last year revenue reached $1.32 million. Ravi uses a democratic leadership style: a works council meets every Friday and staff ideas shaped last year's new yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12%.

Glenmore has just won a contract requiring 22,000 litres a day from January, needing a new pasteuriser costing $85,000. The launch schedule allows only 6 weeks. Ravi is weighing a switch to autocratic leadership so he can impose decisions quickly, or keeping the democratic style workers are used to despite slower meetings.

questions.question_text: Define 'autocratic leadership'.
questions.model_answer: Autocratic leadership is a style of leadership where the leader makes decisions alone without consulting employees and issues clear, direct instructions that staff are expected to follow. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Leader makes decisions alone/without consulting employees
Clear one-way instructions/close control of subordinates

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of a democratic leadership style for Glenmore Dairy Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Democratic leadership involves employees in decision-making, so employee ideas are used [k]; Glenmore staff suggested the new yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12% [app]. Advantage 2: Employees who are consulted often feel valued, raising morale and motivation [k]; the Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged in daily operations [app].

knowledge_max_2: Employees are involved in/consulted about decisions
Involvement can raise motivation/morale/commitment
application_max_2: Staff-suggested new yoghurt flavour lifted sales by 12%
Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of Glenmore Dairy Co switching to an autocratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Autocratic leaders decide alone, so employees lose influence over decisions affecting their work [k]; Ravi's Friday works council, where the 46 employees currently influence decisions, would be pushed aside [app], which could lower morale and cause staff to resist the change [an]. Problem 2: Decisions made without consultation ignore useful employee input [k]; staff knowledge of pasteurising and packing shaped the yoghurt flavour that raised sales [app], so ignoring it risks weaker decisions on the new line and delays the ramp-up to 22,000 litres a day [an].

knowledge_max_2: Autocratic style means the leader decides alone/little employee input
Consultation brings useful employee knowledge/ideas
application_max_2: Friday works council where 46 employees influence decisions
Staff knowledge of pasteurising and packing shaped the yoghurt flavour
analysis_max_2: Lower morale, resistance to change, possible higher labour turnover
Weaker decisions/delays in ramping up to 22,000 litres a day

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravi should switch Glenmore Dairy Co to autocratic leadership for the new contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One reason for switching is speed: autocratic leadership means the leader decides alone and issues direct instructions [k]; the new contract requires 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks and a pasteuriser costing $85,000, so fast unquestioned decisions could keep the launch on schedule [app], reducing the risk of late delivery penalties and protecting the $1.32 million revenue base [an]. However, Glenmore's democratic culture produced the staff-suggested yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12%, and the Friday works council keeps 46 employees committed [k]; sidelining it now could lower motivation just when extra effort is needed for the ramp-up [app], so errors and staff turnover could rise precisely when reliability matters most [an]. On balance, a time-limited use of tighter direction during the 6-week launch makes sense, with democratic consultation restored once running [eval], because permanent autocratic control would damage the culture that made the yoghurt launch successful [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Autocratic leadership = quick unilateral decisions/direct instructions
Democratic leadership = consultation/employee involvement, stronger commitment
application_max_2: 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks; pasteuriser costing $85,000
Yoghurt flavour lifted sales by 12%; Friday works council; 46 employees
analysis_max_2: Faster decisions keep launch on schedule/protect contract and revenue
Sidelining consultation risks lower morale, errors and turnover during ramp-up
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (speed of autocratic vs motivational benefits of democratic)
Justified recommendation: time-limited autocracy, then return to democratic

scenario_stem:
Cypress Bay Hotel Co is a private limited company in Country X operating a 60-room coastal hotel. General manager Paula Duarte leads 28 staff across reception, housekeeping, kitchen and events, with revenue of $1.05 million last year and a gross profit of $410,000. Paula uses a democratic leadership style, holding a weekly 30-minute briefing where employees raise ideas; staff redesigned the breakfast menu this year, raising sales by 9%.

The events manager has resigned and Paula must choose a replacement. Marco, a reception supervisor, would continue her democratic style with the 6-person events team. An external candidate, Lidia, would use a laissez-faire style, giving the experienced team freedom to run events themselves. The events calendar is fully booked with 14 weddings between May and September, and wedding customers pay $12,000 deposits each.

questions.question_text: Define 'democratic leadership'.
questions.model_answer: Democratic leadership is a leadership style where the leader consults employees and involves them in decision-making, using their views before deciding. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Leader consults/involves employees in decisions
Decisions consider employee views before being made

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of democratic leadership for Cypress Bay Hotel Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Democratic leaders share decision-making with employees, using their ideas [k]; staff redesigned the breakfast menu, which raised sales by 9% [app]. Advantage 2: Involvement in decisions can improve morale and commitment [k]; the weekly 30-minute briefing keeps Paula's 28 staff engaged across reception, housekeeping, kitchen and events [app].

knowledge_max_2: Decisions are shared/employees consulted, so ideas are used
Involvement can raise morale/commitment/motivation
application_max_2: Staff redesigned the breakfast menu, raising sales by 9%
Weekly 30-minute briefing keeps 28 staff engaged

questions.question_text: Explain two problems a laissez-faire style could cause for Cypress Bay's events team.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders give employees freedom with little guidance or support [k]; Lidia would let the 6-person events team run weddings with minimal direction [app], so tasks could be missed during the busy season when 14 weddings overlap [an]. Problem 2: Without regular checking, standards can slip [k]; the team would oversee events where customers pay $12,000 deposits with little supervision [app], raising the risk of complaints or refund demands that cut gross profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire = minimal guidance, full freedom for employees
Little monitoring leads to inconsistent standards
application_max_2: 6-person events team given freedom over weddings
$12,000 deposits at stake with little supervision
analysis_max_2: Missed tasks/delays during overlap of 14 weddings
Complaints/refund demands reducing gross profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Paula should promote Marco, the democratic supervisor, or appoint Lidia, the laissez-faire external candidate, as events manager? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lidia would give the experienced 6-person events team freedom to manage the 14 weddings themselves [k]; with the calendar booked between May and September and customers paying $12,000 deposits, empowered staff could respond flexibly to each couple's wishes [app], protecting customer satisfaction and repeat business [an]. However, Marco's democratic style matches the hotel's existing culture: Paula's weekly briefing kept 28 staff engaged and staff ideas lifted breakfast sales by 9% [k]; promoting Marco would preserve consistency, and he already knows the weddings schedule and hotel standards [app], avoiding disruption in the busiest trading season [an]. On balance, promoting Marco with an agreed plan to give the events team more autonomy as the season develops is the safer choice [eval], because Lidia's hands-off style risks uneven delivery if any of the 6 staff falls behind on a May wedding [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire gives autonomy to skilled, experienced staff
Democratic keeps consultation/consistency with existing culture
application_max_2: 14 weddings between May and September; $12,000 deposits
Marco's democratic approach; weekly briefing; breakfast sales up 9%; 28 staff
analysis_max_2: Autonomy improves responsiveness and customer satisfaction
Consistency reduces disruption/errors during peak season
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both candidates/styles
Justified recommendation (promote Marco with phased autonomy)

scenario_stem:
Seaward Printworks is a private limited company in Country X producing marketing brochures, packaging and catalogues for 25 business customers. It is led by production director Omar Haddad, who manages 22 printers and finishers. Output last year was 940,000 printed items, with revenue of $1.28 million and unit costs of $0.86.

Omar has always kept close control of daily schedules. He now employs 5 senior designers who are highly skilled and self-motivated, and they complain that his daily checks slow them down. Omar is deciding whether to move to a laissez-faire style for the design team, letting them set their own deadlines and client meetings, or keep close control until the end of the year, when a $95,000 digital press is installed.

questions.question_text: Define 'laissez-faire leadership'.
questions.model_answer: Laissez-faire leadership is a leadership style where the leader gives employees freedom to make their own decisions and organise their own work, with very little supervision or guidance. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Employees given freedom to make decisions/organise their own work
Little supervision/guidance from the leader

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of laissez-faire leadership for Seaward Printworks.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives employees freedom to organise their own work [k]; Seaward's 5 senior designers could set schedules around each client brief instead of waiting for daily checks [app]. Advantage 2: Autonomy can raise motivation and creativity among skilled staff [k]; the designers would have freedom to propose layouts for the brochures and catalogues, where fresh ideas win print contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: Freedom/autonomy to organise own work with minimal supervision
Autonomy can raise motivation/creativity
application_max_2: 5 senior designers could set schedules around client briefs
Design ideas for brochures and catalogues win print contracts

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of Seaward Printworks adopting a laissez-faire style for the design team.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders avoid close monitoring, so poor work can go unnoticed [k]; the 5 senior designers could miss deadlines on client jobs without Omar's daily checks [app], leading to late delivery to one of the 25 business customers [an]. Problem 2: Inconsistent standards can reduce quality [k]; with no review before files reach the press, errors could pass into production [app], wasting output and reprints against the $1.28 million revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire leaders avoid monitoring, so problems go unnoticed
Inconsistent standards reduce quality
application_max_2: 5 senior designers may miss client-job deadlines without daily checks
Errors could pass into production without review
analysis_max_2: Late delivery damages relations with the 25 business customers
Reprints/waste cut revenue of $1.28 million

questions.question_text: Do you think Omar should move the design team to laissez-faire working now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Omar should give the design team laissez-faire freedom now because the 5 senior designers are highly skilled and self-motivated [k]; removing daily checks would let them meet client briefs faster and improve the brochures and catalogues behind the $1.28 million revenue [app], lifting motivation and the quality of creative work [an]. However, the $95,000 digital press arriving at year-end will change workflows and client expectations [k]; keeping close control until then would let Omar set standards consistently during the changeover [app], avoiding costly mistakes when the new press is commissioned [an]. On balance, a middle path of agreed weekly reviews instead of daily checks until the press is installed captures most of the motivation benefit while limiting risk [eval], and would still protect the 940,000 printed items during the transition [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire frees skilled, self-motivated staff to self-manage
Close control suits periods of change/new equipment installation
application_max_2: 5 senior designers highly skilled/self-motivated; daily checks slow them
$95,000 digital press at year-end; 940,000 printed items; $1.28 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Freedom lifts motivation, speed and design quality
Close control reduces errors during the press changeover
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (freedom now vs control until year-end)
Justified recommendation (weekly reviews until press installed)

scenario_stem:
Coppergrove Assembly Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling small household kitchen appliances. It employs 54 workers on two production lines, producing 3,800 units a month with revenue of $2.1 million last year. Shift supervisor Adam Kone ran the lines under a laissez-faire style, giving workers freedom and rarely interfering.

Output has fallen to 3,400 units a month and error rates have risen from 2% to 5%. New production manager Lucia Ferreira wants to introduce a democratic style with daily 10-minute briefings and worker input on targets, while Adam argues freedom keeps experienced line staff motivated. Adam has run the lines for 6 years, and the line staff trust him. Lucia estimates her plan could restore output to 3,800 units within 3 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'motivation'.
questions.model_answer: Motivation is the internal desire or willingness of employees to work hard and perform well in order to achieve business objectives. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Motivation is the willingness/desire to work hard/perform well
Motivation drives effort towards business objectives

questions.question_text: Explain two ways motivation affects the performance of Coppergrove Assembly Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: A motivated workforce is more productive and achieves higher output [k]; this matters because output has fallen from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month [app]. Point 2: Motivated workers take more care and make fewer mistakes [k]; with the error rate up from 2% to 5%, fewer errors would save wasted appliances [app].

knowledge_max_2: Motivated workers are more productive/achieve higher output
Motivated workers make fewer errors/higher quality work
application_max_2: Output has fallen from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month
Error rate has risen from 2% to 5%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of laissez-faire leadership shown by Coppergrove Assembly Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders provide little guidance or control, so workers may lack direction and standards [k]; under Adam's freedom the lines slipped from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month [app], showing output was not being maintained [an]. Problem 2: Without intervention, quality drifts [k]; errors rose from 2% to 5% with nobody correcting working methods [app], increasing waste and eating into the $2.1 million revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Little guidance/control from laissez-faire leaders
Quality declines without supervision/intervention
application_max_2: Lines slipped from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month
Error rate rose from 2% to 5% without correction
analysis_max_2: Falling productivity/output against targets
More waste/rework reducing revenue of $2.1 million

questions.question_text: Do you think Lucia should introduce democratic leadership at Coppergrove Assembly Ltd? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Democratic leadership involves workers in decisions through consultation and shared information [k]; Lucia's daily 10-minute briefings would let the 54 line workers discuss targets and contribute ideas [app], which should rebuild commitment and could return output to 3,800 units within 3 months [an]. However, Adam argues the experienced line staff value the freedom they already have and their motivation relies on it [k]; replacing freedom with daily briefings could resent workers who prefer autonomy [app], so motivation might fall further before it improves, with errors possibly worsening [an]. On balance, introducing democratic briefings while keeping some team freedom, and reviewing progress after 3 months against the 3,800-unit target, is the better choice [eval], because the democratic approach directly addresses why output fell without removing autonomy completely [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Democratic = consultation/shared decision-making
Laissez-faire = freedom/autonomy valued by experienced staff
application_max_2: Daily 10-minute briefings; worker input on targets; 54 line workers
Output fell to 3,400 units; error rate 5%; target 3,800 within 3 months
analysis_max_2: Involvement rebuilds commitment and output
Abrupt removal of freedom may demotivate and raise resistance
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (democratic briefings vs existing laissez-faire freedom)
Justified recommendation with review period/partial autonomy retained

scenario_stem:
Gannet Logistics Ltd is a private limited company running a distribution depot in Country X. It employs 96 warehouse operatives and drivers on night and day shifts, moving about 1,450 pallets a week. Revenue last year was $6.4 million. Wages start at $11.80 per hour, and last year 23 operatives left the company. The night shift runs from 10pm to 6am, and Gannet pays a $1.90 night-shift allowance on top of the base rate.

A union, the Country X Transport Workers Union (CXTWU), has approached Gannet asking to be recognised for collective bargaining on pay and night-shift allowances. Managing director Sana Iqbal is unsure: recognition could mean higher wage bills, but she worries about recruitment and morale. She must decide within 8 weeks whether to agree.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade union'.
questions.model_answer: A trade union is an organisation of workers formed to protect and advance their members' interests, such as pay, conditions and job security, by negotiating collectively with employers. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Organisation of workers/employees
Protects/advances members' interests (pay, conditions) via collective negotiation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why employees at Gannet Logistics Ltd might want to join the CXTWU.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A trade union negotiates collectively on behalf of members, giving them a stronger voice than negotiating alone [k]; 96 operatives and drivers could together bargain for better night-shift allowances than any one worker could [app]. Reason 2: Unions provide members with advice and representation in disputes [k]; with 23 operatives leaving last year, staff may want union support on pay and conditions issues [app].

knowledge_max_2: Collective bargaining gives a stronger voice than individual negotiation
Advice/representation/support in disputes or grievances
application_max_2: 96 operatives and drivers bargaining for night-shift allowances
23 operatives left last year; pay and conditions concerns

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Gannet Logistics Ltd of its employees joining the CXTWU.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: The business may face pressure to raise pay [k]; recognition for collective bargaining on pay could push the $11.80 hourly wage upward [app], raising labour costs against revenue of $6.4 million [an]. Effect 2: A union can improve communication and handling of grievances [k]; formalising representation could address the causes behind 23 operatives leaving [app], lowering recruitment and training costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: Union pressure pushes up pay/wage bills
Union involvement can improve grievance handling/communication
application_max_2: Collective bargaining on the $11.80 hourly wage and night-shift allowances
Representation could address why 23 operatives left
analysis_max_2: Higher labour costs squeeze profit margins
Better relations/higher retention saves recruitment and training costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Sana should recognise the trade union at Gannet Logistics Ltd? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Sana should recognise the union because members can negotiate collectively for fair pay and conditions [k]; the union's proposal targets pay and night-shift allowances for the 96 employees on $11.80 per hour [app], which could raise morale and reduce the loss of 23 operatives a year, saving recruitment and training costs [an]. However, recognition could raise labour costs: the union may push wages above $11.80 per hour across 1,450 pallets a week [k]; higher settlements and possible industrial action during disputes could disrupt the depot and squeeze the $6.4 million revenue [app], which could force price rises or job losses [an]. On balance, recognising the union with a clear bargaining framework is the better option [eval], because the turnover cost of 23 leavers a year and the value of fair treatment outweigh manageable negotiation costs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Collective bargaining gives members a stronger, unified voice
Recognition can raise wage bills and dispute costs
application_max_2: Pay and night-shift allowances; 96 employees on $11.80 per hour
23 operatives left last year; 1,450 pallets a week; $6.4 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Better morale, lower turnover and reduced recruitment/training costs
Higher wages and possible disruption squeeze margins
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (recognition benefits vs higher costs/disruption)
Justified recommendation (recognise with clear bargaining framework)

scenario_stem:
Mallowgate Flour Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating a flour mill employing 118 workers. It produces 240 tonnes of flour a week for bakeries nationwide, with revenue of $5.6 million last year. The National Mill and Food Workers Union (NMFWU) represents 74 of the workers.

The union balloted members: 81% voted for strike action over pay and the 40-minute unpaid lunch break. Mallowgate has offered a 2.5% pay rise, but the union demands 6% and paid breaks. Formal talks broke down after 7 weeks of negotiation in November. A 10-day strike is planned from 2 December, with the mill holding a contract worth $900,000 a year to supply a national bakery chain, Country X's largest bread buyer.

questions.question_text: Define 'industrial action'.
questions.model_answer: Industrial action is action taken by employees, such as a strike or a work-to-rule, to pressure their employer during an industrial dispute, usually organised through a trade union. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Action by employees/workers against the employer (e.g. strike)
Taken to pressure the employer during a dispute, usually via a trade union

questions.question_text: Explain two effects industrial action could have on Mallowgate Flour Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Industrial action halts or slows production [k]; a 10-day strike would stop the mill producing its 240 tonnes of flour a week [app], so orders for the national bakery chain worth $900,000 a year may not be fulfilled. Effect 2: Industrial action damages reputation and customer confidence [k]; bakeries relying on weekly flour supplies may switch to rival mills during a 10-day stoppage [app], risking the loss of long-term customers and revenue.

knowledge_max_2: Industrial action stops/slows production
Industrial action damages reputation/customer confidence
application_max_2: 10-day strike would stop 240 tonnes a week of flour
Bakery chain contract worth $900,000 a year at risk

questions.question_text: Explain two effects a strike would have on the employees of Mallowgate Flour Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Striking workers lose pay for days not worked [k]; during a 10-day strike from 2 December the 74 union members would forfeit wages while the dispute continues [app], squeezing household budgets even though the 6% demand is the union's goal [an]. Effect 2: Industrial action shows solidarity and strengthens the union's bargaining position [k]; with 81% of voting members backing the strike, the union negotiates from a position of strength [app], increasing the chance the employer improves the 2.5% offer or grants paid breaks [an].

knowledge_max_2: Strikers lose pay for days not worked
Industrial action demonstrates solidarity/strengthens bargaining position
application_max_2: 10-day strike from 2 December; 74 union members would forfeit wages
81% of voting members backed the strike; 2.5% offer vs 6% demand
analysis_max_2: Financial hardship/loss of income for striking workers
Stronger position to win a better offer (6% or paid breaks)

questions.question_text: Do you think Mallowgate Flour Ltd should agree to the union's demands of a 6% pay rise and paid lunch breaks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Agreeing would end the threat to stop production [k]; a settlement would protect the bakery-chain contract worth $900,000 a year and keep 240 tonnes a week flowing [app], avoiding the $5.6 million revenue base being disrupted by a 10-day stoppage [an]. However, conceding 6% is far above the 2.5% offered, and paid breaks add hours that currently go unpaid [k]; lifting the offer to 6% across 118 workers and adding paid breaks would materially raise the wage bill [app], which could force price rises or job cuts at the mill [an]. On balance, Mallowgate should negotiate a compromise, such as a phased rise reaching 6% over two years with a shorter paid break [eval], because outright refusal guarantees a 10-day stoppage while full capitulation sets a costly precedent [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Industrial action pressures the employer; settlement protects production
Concession raises wage costs and may set a precedent for future claims
application_max_2: $900,000 a year bakery-chain contract; 240 tonnes a week; 10-day strike risk
2.5% offer vs 6% demand; 118 workers; $5.6 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Settlement avoids stopped production, lost orders and lost revenue
Full concession strains margins and invites further claims
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (concede fully vs refuse vs compromise)
Justified recommendation: negotiated compromise/phased settlement

scenario_stem:
Hollymoor Garment Co is a private limited company in Country X employing 132 machinists and cutters in one factory. Annual revenue is $3.7 million and the factory produces 26,000 garments a month. The Garment Workers Union represents 98 employees.

Workers have complained about noise averaging 88 decibels near the cutting machines and poor ventilation. The union wants the company to sign a collective agreement covering ear protection, extraction fans and a joint health and safety committee, estimated at $52,000. Director Elena Petrova must decide whether to sign the agreement or keep the current basic safety measures. She has two weeks to respond before the union calls a meeting of all 132 employees. The factory runs two full shifts daily and cannot afford production stoppages.

questions.question_text: Define 'collective bargaining'.
questions.model_answer: Collective bargaining is the process by which a trade union negotiates with an employer on behalf of all its members to agree pay, working hours and conditions of employment. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Union negotiates with employer on behalf of members
Agreement covers pay/working hours/conditions for the group

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of collective bargaining for workers at Hollymoor Garment Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Collective bargaining lets the union negotiate on behalf of all members, giving workers more power than negotiating alone [k]; the 98 employees the union represents could jointly press for ear protection and extraction fans rather than complaining individually [app]. Benefit 2: Collective agreements can fix clear, agreed standards [k]; a signed deal with a joint committee would make the noise target and ventilation arrangements binding on the company [app].

knowledge_max_2: Union negotiates on behalf of members, stronger together
Agreements fix clear, binding standards
application_max_2: 98 employees represented; joint press for ear protection and extraction fans
Joint health and safety committee would make arrangements binding

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Hollymoor Garment Co of signing the health and safety agreement.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Signing the agreement increases short-term costs [k]; ear protection, extraction fans and a joint committee are estimated at $52,000 [app], reducing profit against annual revenue of $3.7 million [an]. Effect 2: A safer workplace can reduce accidents, absences and staff turnover [k]; cutting noise from 88 decibels and improving ventilation would make machinists healthier [app], protecting output of 26,000 garments a month [an].

knowledge_max_2: Agreed safety measures raise short-term costs
Safer workplaces reduce accidents, absence and turnover
application_max_2: $52,000 estimated cost against revenue of $3.7 million
Noise at 88 decibels; ventilation; 26,000 garments a month
analysis_max_2: Lower profit/higher costs in the short term
Healthier, more stable workforce protects output

questions.question_text: Do you think Elena should sign the collective health and safety agreement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing the agreement would address a serious, immediate risk and show the business values its workers [k]; the $52,000 for ear protection, extraction fans and a joint committee is about 1.4% of annual revenue of $3.7 million [app], which is affordable and would tackle the 88-decibel noise directly, cutting accidents, absence and possible compensation claims while protecting 26,000 garments a month [an]. However, a signed collective agreement sets a formal precedent of joint decision-making [k]; once the health and safety committee exists, the company must consult on future changes, and ongoing costs could rise beyond the $52,000 initial estimate [app], limiting management flexibility [an]. On balance, Elena should sign the agreement because the safety risk is measurable at 88 decibels and the cost is modest relative to revenue [eval]; the alternative of waiting for an injury could mean costs far above $52,000 plus reputational damage [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Safer workplace protects employees and reduces absence/accidents
Collective agreements create ongoing consultation obligations
application_max_2: $52,000 ≈ 1.4% of $3.7 million revenue
88-decibel noise; 26,000 garments a month; 98 union employees
analysis_max_2: Prevents accidents/claims and protects output and reputation
Ongoing committee costs and reduced management flexibility
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (sign vs keep current measures)
Justified recommendation (sign) with cost justification

scenario_stem:
Cove & Crumb Café is a private limited company in Country X operating 4 cafés in two seaside towns. It employs 34 staff, including 11 baristas on $9.60 an hour: 7 full-time and 4 part-time. Union membership at the cafés stands at 18 staff. Revenue last year was $1.9 million, and the union has campaigned for the new national minimum wage of $10.25 an hour, effective 1 April.

Owner Dana Whitlock must decide whether to raise the 11 baristas to $10.25 an hour now and absorb the extra cost, or offset it by cutting 40 staff hours a week across the four cafés. July is the peak month with revenue of $310,000, and the cafés trade 11 hours a day on summer tourists.

questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: The minimum wage is the lowest hourly rate of pay that employers are legally required to pay workers, set by the government to protect low-paid employees. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage is a legal minimum hourly pay rate
Set by government to protect/benefit low-paid workers

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the minimum wage rise on workers at Cove & Crumb Café.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Low-paid workers receive higher pay [k]; the 11 baristas currently on $9.60 an hour will earn at least $10.25 from 1 April [app]. Effect 2: Higher pay can improve living standards and motivation [k]; better wages may reduce turnover among the 34 staff who rely on café wages [app].

knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage raises pay for the lowest-paid workers
Higher pay can improve living standards/motivation
application_max_2: 11 baristas rise from $9.60 to $10.25 an hour from 1 April
34 staff rely on café wages; union campaigned for the rise

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the minimum wage rise could cause for Cove & Crumb Café.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Labour costs rise [k]; raising 11 baristas from $9.60 to $10.25 adds cost across the four cafés on revenue of $1.9 million [app], which could force price increases or tighter margins [an]. Problem 2: To control costs the business may cut hours [k]; removing 40 staff hours a week across the cafés would stretch remaining staff during 11-hour days [app], causing longer queues in July and dissatisfied tourists [an].

knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage raises labour/operating costs
Businesses may respond by cutting hours/jobs/prices rise
application_max_2: 11 baristas rising from $9.60 to $10.25; $1.9 million revenue
40 staff hours a week cut; 11-hour trading days; July peak
analysis_max_2: Tighter margins or price increases reduce competitiveness
Understaffing causes queues and lost tourist sales in July

questions.question_text: Do you think Dana should absorb the minimum wage increase or cut 40 staff hours a week to offset it? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Brightcall Teleservices Ltd is a private limited company in Country X running a call centre handling insurance claims. It employs 48 call agents serving 1,300 calls a day, averaging 6 minutes per call, with a complaint rate of 3.2% this quarter. Staff earn $11.40 an hour. Revenue last year was $3.4 million.

Team leader Maya Lindqvist must introduce a new claims script after a regulator's review. Maya has managed the team for 4 years, and the agents respect her. She could impose it autocratically with immediate mandatory compliance and daily checks, or consult agents democratically for 3 weeks before launch. The regulator expects the script live within 5 weeks, and agents have suggested better wording they believe will cut complaints.

Advantage 2: Consultation can improve morale and acceptance of change [k]; discussing the script over 3 weeks would make the 48 call agents more willing to use it properly [app].
